title: Bumped from your flight? Here's exactly what you're owed
summary: Bumped from an overbooked flight? Here's what EC 261 pays, when it applies, and how to claim — plus how the AirHelp app checks it for you.
body_markdown:
Elena was standing at her gate in Warsaw, boarding pass already scanned, when she heard her name over the tannoy — not to board, but to come to the desk. Her flight to Toronto, connecting through Amsterdam, was oversold, and there wasn't a seat for her. Her first thought was that this was just bad luck: rebook, wait around, move on. What she didn't realise yet was that she was standing on one of the few flight problems with a fixed, guaranteed payout attached — set by law, whatever she'd paid for her ticket. Here's exactly what Elena was owed, when it applies, and how to get it, without wading through the regulation yourself.


## What you're owed, at a glance


Flight distance


Compensation


Up to 1,500 km


€250


1,500 to 3,500 km (and any flight between two EU airports, whatever the distance)


€400


Over 3,500 km


€600


Paid regardless of your ticket price — economy or business, same amount. Airlines can halve this if they reroute you and you still land within 2 hours (short-haul), 3 hours (medium-haul), or 4 hours (long-haul) of your original arrival time.


## When this applies — and when it doesn't


Elena's case was actually pretty simple: she'd checked in, she was at the gate on time, and the airline just couldn't seat her — it had sold more tickets than it had seats for. That's involuntary denied boarding, and it's covered. In general, you're covered whenever you had a confirmed reservation, checked in by the deadline, and showed up at the gate on time, but the airline still couldn't get you on the plane (whether that's overbooking, a smaller aircraft, or a crew shortage).


It stops being covered in a few specific situations:


-


You accepted the airline's offer to give up your seat voluntarily — you're covered by whatever you negotiated instead, not by the amounts above.


-


Your travel documents weren't in order (expired passport, missing visa).


-


You were denied boarding for health, safety, or security reasons.


-


You simply didn't reach the gate on time.


One thing airlines sometimes get wrong at the gate: overbooking is not an "extraordinary circumstance." That defence is reserved for things genuinely outside the airline's control — a storm, a security incident, an air traffic control strike. Overbooking is a seating decision the airline made when it sold the ticket, so it can't lean on the same excuse it would use for bad weather.


The EC 261 reform that Parliament and the Council formally signed off in July 2026 doesn't touch any of this — denied boarding and the €250–€600 bands stay exactly as they are (see our[full breakdown of the reform](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/blog/what-ec261-reform-means-for-you/) ). The update mainly adds tarmac-delay and baggage protections, and none of it takes effect before the second half of 2027.


### Elena's case: the leg you're bumped from isn't always the leg that counts


Back to Elena. She was only bumped from the short Amsterdam–Toronto connection, so it would be easy to assume her payout was based on that short hop. It wasn't. EC 261 calculates distance using the last destination the denial delays you from reaching on time — in Elena's case, Toronto, not Amsterdam. So a passenger bumped from what looks like a routine short-haul connection can still be owed the full long-haul amount, because the disruption affects the whole journey, not just the segment where it happened.


It works the other way too: get bumped from the first leg of a long trip but still land at your final destination close to on schedule, and compensation drops or disappears — because what matters legally is your arrival time at the end, not the inconvenience at the gate. Don't calculate your own payout from the leg you were bumped off; base it on your full itinerary. Elena didn't do that maths herself — she described what happened to the AirHelp app, and it worked out from her booking reference that she was owed the full long-haul amount, not a short-haul one.


## What to do if you're bumped


1.


Don't jump at the first offer. If the airline asks for volunteers, ask what they're offering before you agree — once you volunteer, you give up the fixed statutory amount for whatever you negotiate instead.


2.


Ask for it in writing. Airlines must give you a written notice explaining your rights and how compensation is calculated. Get it before you leave the airport.


3.


Get your care while you wait. Meals, refreshments, and — if you're overnighting — a hotel and transport are separate from compensation and not conditional on it.


4.


Choose rerouting or a refund. Take the next available flight, or walk away with your money back if the trip is no longer useful to you.


5.


Keep everything. Boarding pass, booking reference, the written notice, and receipts for anything you paid for yourself.


6.


File the claim. You don't need a lawyer — most claims are a flight-details form and some patience.


## How to claim


The mechanics of filing — what counts as valid proof, how airlines are allowed to respond, and what happens if they push back — are covered in full on our[denied boarding compensation page](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/denied-boarding-compensation/) , along with the rules for[overbooking specifically on our overbooked flight compensation page](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/overbooking-compensation/) . If you'd rather skip the paperwork, the AirHelp app checks your eligibility in under a minute: describe what happened in plain language, and it works out your route, your flight, and your estimated payout, without asking for personal details up front. If you're eligible, you can start the claim straight from the result screen — AirHelp[handles the airline from there.](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/blog/how-to-use-airhelp-to-claim-flight-compensation/)


## Frequently asked questions


#### Does denied boarding compensation depend on how much I paid for my ticket?


No. The amount is fixed by flight distance — €250, €400, or €600 — and is the same whether you flew economy or business class.


#### What happens if I volunteer to give up my seat?


You lose the right to the statutory amount and instead get whatever the airline offers you in exchange — cash, vouchers, or a later flight. Read the offer carefully before you agree; there's no legal minimum for voluntary denied boarding.


#### Can the airline refuse and call it an "extraordinary circumstance"?


Not for overbooking. Extraordinary circumstances cover things like severe weather or security incidents — genuinely outside the airline's control. Overbooking is a commercial decision the airline made, so it doesn't qualify as an excuse.


#### How long do I have to file a denied boarding claim?


This varies by country — some allow several years. Don't wait to find out: file as soon as you can, and keep your documents in the meantime.
